extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; scholars of Hobbes and early modern natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Hobbes' account of imagination, memory, speech, names, understanding, reason, science, and causes of absurdity — i.e., what counts as correct use of words and right reasoning. Useful for analyzing standards for clear definition, method, and valid inference in philosophical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of regulated thought / invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The train of regulated Thoughts is of two kinds: (1) when, of an effect imagined, we seek the causes or means that produce it (common to man and beast); (2) when imagining anything whatsoever, we seek all the possible effects that can be produced by it (curiosity proper to man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second kind — the faculty of Invention (Sagacitas, Solertia) — is characteristic of man and consists in hunting out causes of some effect present or past, or effects of some present or past cause. Examples: seeking what one lost by running thoughts back over places/times; sweeping a room or a spaniel ranging a field; running over the alphabet to start a rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remembrance
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembrance (Calling to mind) is when a man, seeking something lost, runs his mind back from the place and time he misses it to find a certain limited time and place in which to begin a method of seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remembrance consists in running thoughts over places and times to find what action or occasion made one lose the thing — likened to sweeping a room or a spaniel ranging the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence / Foresight
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence (Foresight, Providence, sometimes Wisdom) is the thinking of some like past action and its events, supposing similar events will follow similar actions, to predict future outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence is grounded on experience: the more one has observed past events, the more prudent one will be and the more reliable expectations will be — yet still fallacious due to unobserved circumstances. The Future has no being in nature; it is a fiction of the mind applying past sequels to present actions. True prophecy belongs only to God; natural prophecy is best-guessing based on many signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs (signes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sign is the event antecedent of the consequent (or conversely) when like consequences have been observed before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more often antecedent-consequent pairings have been observed, the less uncertain the sign. Thus experience confers more signs and hence greater prudence in guessing the future. Example: someone versed in a kind of business has more signs to predict outcomes than a novice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjecture of the time past
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference about past events from other past things (e.g., from the ruins of a state to guess it underwent civil war and ruin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conjecture has almost the same uncertainty as conjecture about the future because both are grounded only on experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of imagination / finiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever we imagine is finite; there is no idea or conception in the mind of anything infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No man can have an image of infinite magnitude or conceive ends/bounds of the thing named; names like 'GOD' are used not to make us conceive him but to honor. Conceptions derive from sense, so nothing not subject to sense can be conceived without being absurd or crediting deceived philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and chief use of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech (consisting of names/apellations and their connexion) is the most noble and profitable invention: it registers thoughts, recalls them, declares them to others for mutual utility and conversation, and makes commonwealth/society possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary uses: (1) register consequences of thoughts (memory), (2) signify to others what we conceive (counsel/teach), (3) make known wills/purposes for mutual help, (4) please/delight by playing with words. Origin anecdote: God instructed Adam to name creatures; language grew thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses of speech (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four corresponding abuses of speech: (1) registering thoughts wrong by inconstancy of signification (self-deception); (2) using words metaphorically (deceiving others); (3) declaring by words a will that is not true; (4) using words to grieve another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using speech to grieve (insult, harm) is an abuse except when used to correct or govern someone one is obliged to govern. Metaphorical/tropological uses are sometimes acceptable in common speech but dangerous for seeking truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names vs common (universal) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names are singular to one thing (e.g., Peter); common names are imposed on many things for their similitude and thus serve as universals recalling any one of those things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All universals exist only as names; things themselves are individual. Universals of larger or smaller extent encompass one another (e.g., Body > Man). A 'name' may be multiple words or circumlocution; correct imposition of names enables universal reasoning (example: triangles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of words to generalize and relieve mental labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Words enable moving from a particular observation to universal rules, thereby discharging mental reckoning of time and place and making conclusions hold in all times/places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: by naming 'triangle' and defining its relevant features, one can conclude universally that three angles equal two right angles. Words are essential for numbering and reckoning (arithmetical sequence), magnitudes, speeds, forces, etc.; without words there is no possibility of such general reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and falsehood as attributes of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: True and False are attributes of Speech, not of things; where speech is not, there is neither truth nor falsehood (though there can be error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To seek precise truth one must remember what every name stands for and place it accordingly; failure leads to being entangled in words and multiplying errors through subsequent reasoning (book errors compound like mis-added sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Settling the significations of words (Definitions) is foundational: in Geometry they begin by defining terms to make subsequent reckoning indisputable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One aspiring to true knowledge must examine prior definitions and correct or make them anew. Wrong definitions multiply errors leading to absurdities; reliance on books without verifying first principles is like casting many little sums into a greater without checking each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: what can be 'subject to names'
rubrics_metrics.description: Things enter into account (subject to names) in four general heads: (1) matter/body (being living, sensible, rational); (2) accidents/qualities conceived in it (heat, length); (3) properties of our own bodies (sight, sound — fancies); (4) names themselves and speeches (general, equivocal, affirmation, syllogism, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy explains how the same thing may be named differently depending on the consideration (matter vs accident vs fancy vs speech), which is a source of confusion if not attended to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative names (their use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative names (Nothing, No Man, Infinite, Indocible) are useful notes signifying that a word is not the name of the thing in question and serve to correct reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative names call to mind past cogitations though they are not names of any thing; they function to refuse admission of wrongly used names in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant words (two kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that are insignificant either (1) are new but undefined (coined by schoolmen/philosophers) or (2) are compounds of names whose significations are contradictory/inconsistent (e.g., 'incorporeal substance', 'round quadrangle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an affirmation is false the compound word made of its terms signifies nothing and is mere sound. Many senseless words in philosophy are derived from Latin/Greek coinages and are meaningless without clear definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as conception caused by speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding occurs when the hearer, upon hearing speech, has the thoughts which the words and their connexion were ordained to signify; Understanding is nothing else but conception caused by Speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If speech is peculiar to man, understanding is too. Absurd or false universal affirmations admit no understanding; mere repetition of words without conception is not understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconstant names due to passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of things that affect us (pleasure/displeasure) have inconstant signification because different people or the same person at different times conceive things differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/valuational words (virtue, cruelty, prodigality, magnanimity, gravity, stupidity) are especially inconstant and cannot serve as true grounds for ratiocination. Metaphors and tropes are less dangerous since they profess inconstancy, but still problematic in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason defined as reckoning of names' consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is nothing but reckoning (adding and subtracting) of the consequences of general names agreed upon for marking and signifying our thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning is analogous to arithmetic and geometry operations: adding names to make an affirmation, combining affirmations to make a syllogism, many syllogisms to make a demonstration. Wherever addition and subtraction of parts applies (numbers, lines, qualities, duties, laws), reason applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right reason requires constituted judge / method
rubrics_metrics.description: No one man's reason nor the reason of any number of men makes certainty; where controversy exists, parties must set up an arbitrator/judge or right reason is undecided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who clamor for 'right Reason' often only demand that things be determined by their own reason. Right reason in society must be constituted (like appointing a judge); otherwise disputes remain unresolved and intolerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of reason: begin at definitions and proceed
rubrics_metrics.description: The use and end of reason is not finding remote consequences but to begin at definitions (elements) and proceed from one consequence to another, securing certainty at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There can be no certainty of the final conclusion without certainty of all antecedent affirmations/negations; taking conclusions on trust of authors without checking first items means one does not know but only believes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error versus absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Error (in particular reckoning without words) is a deception in presuming something past or future; Absurdity is when one reasons in words of general signification and reaches a general inference which is false or speech without meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error admits possibility but is mistaken about occurrence; absurdity is speech without conceivable possibility (e.g., 'round quadrangle', 'immaterial substances', or incoherent 'free' usages). Absurdities stem from false universal assertions or meaningless compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of absurdity (sevenfold list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven causes of absurd conclusions: (1) want of Method — not beginning from Definitions; (2) giving names of Bodies to Accidents or vice versa; (3) giving names of Accidents of bodies without us to the accidents of our own bodies; (4) giving names of Bodies to Names/Speeches (treating universals as things); (5) giving names of Accidents to Names and Speeches; (6) use of Metaphors/Tropes in place of proper words; (7) names that signify nothing (canting scholastic terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these seven faults to escape absurdity; they explain many philosophical confusions. Metaphors may be lawful in common speech but are not to be admitted in seeking truth. Examples: 'Faith is infused', 'Phantasmes are spirits', scholastic terms like 'Hypostatical' causing senseless speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as attained by industry and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is not born with sense and memory or gotten by experience only; it is attained by industry: apt imposing of names and getting a good and orderly method in proceeding from elements (names) to assertions and syllogisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sense and Memory give knowledge of fact; Science is knowledge of consequences and dependencies enabling one to reproduce effects. Children become reasonable only by acquiring speech. Men without science but with natural prudence are in a better condition than those led by false rules or false authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence versus Sapience (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence is much experience; Sapience (wisdom) is much science. Prudence is the practical dexterity from experience; sapience adds acquired science making one's ability far more certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are useful, but those trusting blindly to authority or false rules are like a badly taught fencer who is killed or disgraced. Sapience (science) renders action infallible in principle; prudence alone is fallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Science (some certain, some uncertain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science has signs: some signs are certain and infallible; some are uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text begins to enumerate that sciences vary in the certainty of their signs; more fully developed signs and method produce greater certainty of science (the chapter continues beyond this chunk).
